# Ads Incrementality Check

An ad platform's conversion count tells you who the ad touched before they acted. It does
not tell you who the ad brought. This skill answers the question an owner is paying for:
when the campaign is off, does the phone ring less? It uses a planned pause and a record
the ad platform doesn't control, the business's own phone log. Done means a readout a
skeptic would sign: the measures, the windows, everything else that changed, a verdict
(brings calls, doesn't, can't tell yet) and the money decision that follows. The method is
a floor: a better design for the business in front of you wins, stated in one line.

Three hard rules:

1. **The pause is the owner's decision.** Plan it, show what it could cost if the
   campaign does bring calls, and get a yes. Never pause or resume a campaign without one.
2. **Platform conversions are the claim, never the evidence.** Evidence comes from the
   phone log, the job system, the inbox or the order system.
3. **No verdict the data can't carry.** A short window, overlapping changes or too few
   calls a day earn "can't tell yet", which is a complete answer.

## Context

Only if `./brand/`, `./brands/` or `MARKETING.md` exists (nothing to load otherwise), run:
`python3 ${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/../start-here/scripts/brand_context.py --for ads-incrementality-check`
(`${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}` is this skill's folder; outside Claude Code use the folder this
file was read from, e.g. `.agents/skills/ads-incrementality-check`. If the script or python3 is
unavailable, read the brand folder directly: `./brands/<slug>/` when `./brands/active`
names one, else `./brand/`; then `MARKETING.md`, `preferences.md` and the files in
`reads:`. If none exist, proceed standalone and ask only for: the campaign under suspicion, its monthly
spend, what the platform credits it with, and a call log export covering at least 60 days.)

If `learnings.md` holds an earlier pause result for this business, plan around how this
test differs from it. Mention it only if it changed the plan, as one line in the Sources
and assumptions note.

## When to run it

Any one of these is reason enough:

- One campaign is credited with most of the account's conversions, and those conversions
  are Google-hosted: "Business profile" calls, "Clicks to call", "Get directions".
- Platform conversions climb while booked jobs stay flat.
- Branded search (people typing the business's name), retargeting, or Meta results that
  lean on view-through conversions.
- Before resuming a paused campaign or raising its budget.

**Why local actions over-claim.** Google counts a local action when it follows an ad
interaction within the click-through window (30 days by default), including a later tap on
the business's organic Business Profile. Profile calls that can be tied to an ad
interaction land in "Calls from ads". A known local business gets profile calls every day.
A Performance Max campaign that serves on Maps and on the business's own name touches many
of those people first and collects the credit. Nothing here is fraud. It is attribution
doing what it was built to do, and it is why a count can't answer this question.

**The case this skill came from.**
A home service business ran Performance Max, and Google credited it with most of the account's conversions over three months, almost all Business Profile calls.
The campaign was then paused. Four measures from the business's own records:

| Measure, per day | During the pause |
|---|---|
| Google Business Profile call clicks | About the same |
| Inbound calls, raw | Slightly up |
| Answered inbound calls 30 seconds or longer, main line | Slightly up |
| Unique callers | Unchanged |

Google's claim worked out to several calls a day caused by the campaign.
Not one of the four measures fell. An earlier recommendation to turn the campaign back on, made from
Google's count, was reversed. The readout also said what it couldn't settle: the pause window was
shorter than the month before, season wasn't controlled, and it measured calls, not jobs. The
decision was to keep it paused and recheck after a full month.

## Phase 1: Pick the denominator

For a business where most leads phone in, the phone log is the truth. Pull 60 days or
more before the test from the phone system (Quo or OpenPhone, CallRail, RingCentral, Google
Voice, a carrier portal) and read it into four daily measures:

1. **Inbound calls, raw.** Coarse. Includes spam, misdials and customers calling about
   jobs already booked.
2. **Answered inbound calls 30 seconds or longer, on the lines the public uses.** Strips
   spam, misdials and hang-ups. The single best measure.
3. **Unique callers.** One customer calling five times is one caller.
4. **Google Business Profile call clicks**, from the profile's Performance view, by day
   or week. This is the surface the campaign claims, so it must be in the table.

Two more when the data allows: **new callers** (numbers not seen in the log before), the
closest thing to new customers, and **booked jobs per week** from the job system, the money
measure, slower and noisier.

Run the script on the export. It guesses the columns, prints its guesses, and accepts
overrides:

```
python3 ${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/call_log.py pause-test calls.csv \
  --before 2026-03-02:2026-03-29 --during 2026-03-30:2026-04-26 \
  --after 2026-04-27:2026-05-24 --line "Main" --exclude staff-numbers.txt --utc-offset -6
```

The columns it guessed and the numbers it excluded go in `notes.md`, never in the readout.

Cleaning that changes the answer:

- Filter to the public lines and inbound calls. Drop staff, vendor and known spam numbers.
- Don't count with an automatic call classifier until you've checked its coverage. In the
  case above, the classifier had marked every call in the month "uncertain", so it couldn't support any comparison.
- Expect status calls. A large share of customer calls can be about jobs already in motion (arrival time, invoice, parts).
  Ads don't move those calls. They dilute the signal, which is why unique and new callers
  sit beside the raw count.

**If the business sells online,** the denominator is orders, signups or booked demos from
the store, payment or CRM system, split into new and returning customers. Branded search,
retargeting and view-through conversions are the usual suspects, and the rest of the
method is unchanged.

# AI Search (AEO/GEO)

A growing share of buyers never see a homepage. They see a paragraph an AI assistant wrote about the category, with a few sources cited, or a short list of three to five local businesses with a reason for each. This skill measures whether the business is in that paragraph, diagnoses why the winners are, fixes what's fixable on pages and listings the business already has, and tracks the result. Done means an audit another person could re-run with the same questions, a fix plan ordered by citation leverage, and an honest account of what was observed and what was a proxy. The method is a floor. A better path is welcome with a one-line reason. MONITOR's zero-question contract and the measurement rules below don't flex.

## Context

Only if `./brand/`, `./brands/` or `MARKETING.md` exists (nothing to load otherwise), run:
`python3 ${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/../start-here/scripts/brand_context.py --for ai-search`
(`${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}` is this skill's folder; outside Claude Code use the folder this file was read from, e.g. `.agents/skills/ai-search`. Load `references/aeo-facts.md` before any mode (check its header; refresh if stale). Load `references/aeo-judgment.md` before diagnosis and before any OPTIMIZE recommendation. For a local business, also load `references/local-ai-facts.md` (check its header) and `references/local-prompt-sets.md`.

**Is this a local business?** If it serves customers in places (a trade, a clinic, a shop, a restaurant), run the Local branch wherever it appears below. Otherwise skip it.

## Modes

| Trigger | Mode |
|---|---|
| Default: a domain, a brand name, or nothing | **AUDIT** |
| "optimize", "fix", "llms.txt", "make us citable" | **OPTIMIZE** |
| "monitor", "what changed", or any scheduled or non-interactive run | **MONITOR** |

MONITOR asks zero questions. OPTIMIZE without a prior audit runs a compressed AUDIT first. Quick Mode: a narrow ask ("are we cited for this one question?") gets a single capture and a one-paragraph answer, no files unless asked.

## Measurement rules (all modes)

These are what make an audit worth re-running:
- **Sample, don't sweep.** 10 to 15 questions is the useful range. Freeze them verbatim in the audit; MONITOR repeats exactly that list.
- **Count over what you observed.** Report "named in 7 of 12 observed answers", never "58% visible" over questions you attempted. A question whose answer you couldn't capture is NOT OBSERVED, never ABSENT.
- **Four states per answer and entity:** CITED (its own site is a source), MENTIONED (named, but its site isn't a source, so others tell its story), ABSENT (the answer was observed and it isn't there), NOT OBSERVED.
- **Answers vary run to run.** Repeated runs of the same prompt share only a minority of their sources (figures in `references/aeo-facts.md`). Run the top questions twice or across engines, and treat one run as a sample.
- **Claims are about the answers collected,** not about "what ChatGPT thinks". Say which engine, which date, which location.
- **A failed capture is never a finding.** A timeout, an out-of-credit error or a page that wouldn't load is NOT OBSERVED. One audit tool once counted errors as gaps and told well-known brands they were missing from answers they were in. Never write "you're invisible" over a run with failed or unobserved captures, and never claim a site is blocked or unreadable because your own fetch failed.

### Phase 1. Build the question set

**If `keyword-plan.md` exists,** start from its commercial and comparison families. Rewrite each keyword as the question a buyer would type into an assistant, because the phrasing changes which sources get retrieved. "crm for freelancers" and "what's the best CRM for a solo freelancer?" pull different citation sets; keep both when they plausibly diverge.

Keep the set on one topic when you can. Fifteen questions on the topic the business is committing to beat fifteen spread across everything it sells, because the result has to pick a fix. Include the AI-native forms: the long, conversational questions with near-zero Google volume (from `keyword-plan.md`, `voc.md`, call notes, reviews and forums). They often decide who gets recommended.

**If not,** derive from `positioning.md` across four kinds, skewed toward where the money is:
1. **Category:** "best <category> for <buyer>" (3 to 5)
2. **Comparison:** "<brand> vs <competitor>", "<leader> alternatives" (2 to 4)
3. **Problem:** the pain in the buyer's words before they know the category exists (3 to 4)
4. **Brand:** "what is <brand>", "is <brand> worth it", "<brand> alternatives" (2 to 3)

**Run the entity probe first.** Before the set, ask each engine "what is <brand>?" and "what is <domain>?". If the answer describes a different company, a product with a similar name, or something unrelated, that's the first finding: until the engines tie the name to the site, no content fix compounds. The alternatives question shows who the engines think the brand competes with, which is sometimes not who the brand thinks.

Example, a proposal tool for freelancers: "best proposal software for freelance designers", "<competitor> vs <brand>", "how do I stop clients ghosting after I send a quote", "is <brand> worth it for a solo freelancer".

**Local branch.** Every question names the place: the city, or a neighborhood when the business is in a big metro. A question without a place gets answered for wherever the engine guesses the user is, which makes the result mislabeled evidence. Add two kinds that matter locally: **urgent** ("emergency plumber in Dallas open now") and **cost** ("how much does water heater replacement cost in Dallas"). # Audience Research

Find the rooms where your buyers complain, compare, and confess, and bring back their
exact words. Done means two files: an audience profile where every claim traces to
evidence, and a verbatim language bank that lets every downstream skill enter the
conversation already happening in the customer's head. The judgment this skill carries:
knowing which sources are signal for which business, and refusing to launder paraphrase
as voice-of-customer. The method is a floor, not a ceiling. When the category in front
of you argues for different sources or sequence, take them and say why.

## Context

Only if `./brand/`, `./brands/` or `MARKETING.md` exists (nothing to load otherwise), run:
`python3 ${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/../start-here/scripts/brand_context.py --for audience-research`
(If the script or python3 is unavailable, read the files named in `reads:` directly,
section-anchored where specified. If none exist, proceed standalone. Ask only for what
the task strictly requires.)

If `positioning.md#market-assessment` exists, use its declared `Category:` and the known
competitors as mining seeds. If `audience.md` or `voc.md` already exist (check `brand.yaml`), default to
**Refresh mode** unless the user asks to start over.

## Modes

- **Full research** (default): Phases 1-4 below. Needs a product URL or a one-line
  description + category.
- **Refresh** ("refresh my audience research"): diff new mining against existing files.
  See Refresh mode.
- **Interview fallback**: no URL, web access failing, or the user explicitly wants a fast
  draft. See Interview fallback. The audience.md header carries `Data: MODEL KNOWLEDGE`, and
  the chat note says in plain words that this is a draft from category knowledge, not mined
  research. Never let it masquerade as mined research.
- **Quick Mode**: a narrow ask ("what do customers say about onboarding?", "mine pricing
  objections") gets a targeted mine of 2-3 sources on that theme only, appended to voc.md
  under the matching section. No source map ceremony, no full synthesis. Deliver, then
  one line of what's-next.

## Phase 1: Source map

From the product category, pick **5-8 mining sources**. This is a judgment call, not a
checklist: the wrong sources return polite noise; the right ones return rage, longing,
and exact vocabulary.

Highest-signal sources by business type:

| Business type | Mine first | Also strong | Usually weak |
|---|---|---|---|
| B2B SaaS | G2 + Capterra (2-4★), category subreddits, **competitor G2 reviews** | LinkedIn comment threads, niche Slack/Discord (if public), HN threads | Twitter praise, vendor case studies |
| E-com / consumer product | Amazon reviews (own + competitor, 2-4★), Reddit | Trustpilot, YouTube review comments, TikTok comments | Instagram comments (performative) |
| Mobile / app | App Store + Play Store reviews (sort: recent, not helpful), Reddit | YouTube tutorial comments | The app's own community (survivor bias) |
| Services / agency | Reddit ("anyone hired a...?" threads), X/LinkedIn discussions | Google/Clutch reviews, podcast episode comments | Testimonial pages |
| Local service business | Google reviews (2 to 4 stars) of the business and the top 3 in its map pack, Reddit trade and city threads ("anyone used a good plumber in...?"), Angi, Yelp and BBB complaints | Nextdoor and neighborhood groups when public, Thumbtack | The business's own testimonials page |
| Creator / info product | **YouTube comments on category videos** (not the creator's own), Reddit | X replies under big accounts in the niche, Udemy/Skool reviews of competing courses | The creator's own audience (already converted) |

Rules that govern the map:

- **Local example (sample business Hartline Plumbing, Dallas TX).** Mine its Google reviews and those of the top three plumbers in the map pack, one Dallas thread search ("plumber", "water heater", "overcharged"), and the one-to-three-star Angi or Yelp reviews. The switching triggers are usually showing up late, surprise bills and no callback. Those words become the language for ads and the first screen.
- **Competitor reviews outrank your own.** Your reviews tell you about your product;
  competitor reviews tell you about the market. Competitor 1-star reviews are switching
  triggers verbatim. Default: at least one miner on a competitor review surface.
- **Find the real subreddits, don't guess.** Search `site:reddit.com [category problem
  language]` and verify the sub is alive (posts in the last week, comments per post >3)
  before assigning a miner to it. A dead sub burns a slot. We use Exa for this search:
  it matches on meaning, so a thread that describes the problem in the customer's own
  words comes up even when no keyword matches (free tier, then pay as you go). Without
  it, the `site:reddit.com` search in WebSearch does the job.
- **One source per distinct *conversation type*.** Reviews = post-purchase judgment.
  Reddit/forums = pre-purchase confusion and comparison. YouTube comments = aspiration
  and skepticism. Social = identity and hot takes. You want coverage across types, not
  five review sites.
- 5-8 sources is the budget. If the category is tiny (niche B2B), 4 deep sources beat 8
  thin ones. Say so and proceed.
- Hard caps: each miner ≤ 5 page fetches on its source and ≤ 8 minutes,
  no sub-agents. A miner that hits its cap returns its pack as-is, labelled
  `budget-capped`.

Keep the source map as working notes (source, type, why); it becomes Watering Holes in
audience.md, not chat output. Do not ask permission to mine unless access is ambiguous
(private community, login wall).

## Phase 2: Parallel mining

**Check the web first.** Before dispatching, make sure your own WebSearch works (the
Phase 1 subreddit search counts; otherwise run one). If it is denied or errors, the
miners will be blocked too: don't dispatch them, go to Interview fallback and say why in
one line. If miners come back blocked anyway, do the same with whatever they returned.

We use Firecrawl to read the review and forum pages: full-page reads, so every quote
comes from the page itself and not a summary. It has a free tier of 1,000 credits a month
with no card, and Hobby starts at $16 a month (billed yearly) for 5,000. Without it,
WebFetch reads the public pages; where it returns only a summary, take the quote from the
search result with its full URL or report the skip.

Fan out **one subagent per source**, all in parallel, using the Task/Agent tool
(`general-purpose`). Each subagent's brief must include:

1. The source URL(s)/search strategy, the product, category, and known competitors.
2. Instruction to read `${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/references/voc-mining-judgment.md` before
   mining. It carries the signal/noise rules (2-4★ first, specificity weighting,
   astroturf detection, "I wish it..." flags).
3. Budget: ≤ 5 pag

# Brand Voice

Produce a voice profile specific enough that a stranger holding only the profile writes
content the brand's audience would attribute to the brand, and tight enough that every
line rules something out. The judgment this skill carries: voice claims are
evidence-backed and falsifiable, never horoscope; the Voice Test Loop, not
interrogation, is how the profile gets accurate. The method is a floor, not a ceiling.
When the content in front of you argues for a better path, take it and say why.

## Context

Only if `./brand/`, `./brands/` or `MARKETING.md` exists (nothing to load otherwise), run:
`python3 ${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/../start-here/scripts/brand_context.py --for brand-voice`
(If the script or python3 is unavailable, read the files named in `reads:` directly. If
none exist, proceed standalone: ask only for what the task strictly requires.)

Positioning shapes stance (a rebel brand and a trusted-advisor brand land differently on
every spectrum); audience shapes jargon tolerance and register. Use them as priors,
never as substitutes for evidence.

**Before writing or updating any profile, load `references/voice-extraction-judgment.md`**.
Its falsifiability rule, exhibit-citation requirement, and competitor-paste test are
the quality bar for every line of the profile.

## Modes

| Mode | When | Signal |
|---|---|---|
| **Extract** | They have content they're proud of | Pasted content, file paths, "analyze these" |
| **Build** | No crawlable surface exists, or existing content is deliberately being abandoned | "I don't have content" AND no site/socials to mine |
| **Auto-Scrape** | A crawlable surface exists, whether or not they mentioned it | URL in the message, or a domain/handle findable in brand.yaml / positioning.md / stack.md |
| **Drift Check** | Saved profile exists; they want recent content audited | "drift check," "is this still on brand," recent posts + existing profile |

**Tools pick the mode (extract, don't interview):** when the web-scrape capability is
present, check for a crawlable surface BEFORE asking anything. The message, then
brand.yaml, positioning.md, stack.md for a domain or social handles. Found one →
Auto-Scrape is the first pass, even if they said "help me define my voice": crawl,
extract, present the drafted profile for correction. Build's questions then fill only
the gaps the corpus couldn't answer (usually the anti-model and hard lines). A person
with a live website should never face an interview a crawler could have skipped.

If `./brand/voice-profile.md` already exists and the request isn't Drift Check, this is
an **update**: read the existing profile, apply the requested change or re-extract on
new evidence, run the Voice Test Loop on what changed, then save (auto-version per
`start-here/references/brand-memory.md`; show a 3-line summary of what changed, with no confirmation ceremony).

If no surface is findable and the mode is still ambiguous, ask ONE question: "Do you
have published content that sounds like you, or are we building from scratch? (A URL
works too: I'll do the research.)"

---

## The six dimensions

Every mode analyzes (or constructs) the same six dimensions. These are the skeleton of
the profile.

1. **Tone:** position on five spectrums: Formal↔Casual, Serious↔Playful, Reserved↔Bold,
   Simple↔Sophisticated, Warm↔Direct. A position is only useful with its mechanism
   ("casual in syntax, never in punctuation" beats "pretty casual").
2. **Vocabulary:** signature words and coinages, banned words, jargon level and what
   jargon signals (peer vs seller), profanity policy.
3. **Rhythm:** sentence-length distribution (the mix, not the average), paragraph shape,
   fragment use, where the prose speeds up and slows down.
4. **Structure:** how pieces open (story / claim / question), how they transition, how
   they close (CTA / open loop / cold stop), formatting habits.
5. **Personality:** the 3-4 traits that show up as observable behavior in the prose:
   self-deprecating about what? confident how? teacher or peer? What's the recurring
   move?
6. **POV & address:** I vs we, how the reader is addressed, the relationship stance
   (peer slightly ahead / guide / insider / rebel).

---

## Mode: Extract

Input: 3-5 pieces the user considers "most them": posts, emails, transcripts, pages.
Under ~1,500 words total, say the corpus is too thin for reliable patterns and offer to
Auto-Scrape the gaps or proceed with caveats.

Process:
1. Read everything once for gestalt, then once per dimension.
2. Pull verbatim exhibits (5-60 words each) as you go. Every pattern you think you see
   must be pinned to a quote. Target 10-20 exhibits.
3. Write the profile (template below), citing exhibit IDs per the falsifiability rule.
4. Run the Voice Test Loop.

What separates a good extraction from a mediocre one: the mediocre one describes what
the content is ABOUT; the good one describes what the writer DOES. The repeated move,
the thing they never do, the habit they probably don't know they have. If you can't name
three habits the brand itself would be surprised to see articulated, read the corpus
again.

## Mode: Build

No corpus exists, so don't fake one with 15 questions. Most answers to voice
questionnaires are aspirational noise. Ask the four that actually constrain the profile,
infer everything else, and let the Voice Test Loop catch inference errors (it's cheaper
for the user to react to three sample paragraphs than to answer eleven more questions):

1. **Identity belief:** "What do you believe about your space that most competitors
   wouldn't say out loud?" (This becomes the spine. A voice with nothing to assert
   defaults to mush.)
2. **Anti-model:** "Name a brand or creator you do NOT want to sound like. What
   specifically grates?" (Negative space is more diagnostic than positive aspiration.)
3. **Admired voices:** "2-3 voices you admire (any field) and the one specific thing
   each does that you'd steal."
4. **Audience:** "Who are you talking to, and how do THEY talk?" (Skip if `audience.md`
   already answers it.)

Optionally, a fifth if their answers leave it genuinely open: "Any hard lines:
profanity, humor, hot takes, emoji?"

Then construct: derive the spectrums from belief + anti-model, vocabulary from
admired-voice mechanics + audience language, rhythm and structure as your best inference
from the register they used answering you. Mark the profile `Evidence: INTAKE (exhibits
pending first published content)` and cite their verbatim answers as interim exhibits.
Run the Voice Test Loop. In Build mode it's load-bearing, since the samples are the
first evidence that ever existed.

# Competitive Intel

Competitor pages tell you what they claim; their ads tell you what they'll pay to claim; their pricing tells you who they're built for; their reviews tell you where they break. This skill collects all four in parallel, with verbatim evidence, and turns them into the three gaps you can actually exploit. Done means: a competitors.md another skill can act on without re-researching, where every claim traces to a quote or URL. The method is a floor, not a ceiling. When the category in front of you argues for a better path, take it and say why.

## Context

Only if `./brand/`, `./brands/` or `MARKETING.md` exists (nothing to load otherwise), run:
`python3 ${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/../start-here/scripts/brand_context.py --for competitive-intel`
(`${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}` is this skill's folder; outside Claude Code use the folder this
file was read from, e.g. `.agents/skills/competitive-intel`. If the script or python3 is
unavailable, read the brand folder directly: `./brands/<slug>/` when `./brands/active`
names one, else `./brand/`; then `MARKETING.md`, `preferences.md` and the files in

competitor names (or, for a local business, the main service and city).)

## Modes

| Trigger | Mode |
|---|---|
| Default: names, URLs, a category, or nothing | **TEARDOWN** |
| "watch", "diff", "what changed", or any non-interactive/scheduled invocation | **WATCH** |
| "ads", "ad recon", "what ads are they running" | **AD RECON** |
| A local service business (brand files say so, or the request names a city, "near me" or Google Maps) | **LOCAL** |

WATCH and AD RECON are below the teardown sections. WATCH asks zero questions. It is what the weekly competitor-watch routine calls.

## Mode 1: TEARDOWN (default)

### Phase 1: Build the roster

Target 3-6 competitors. Resolve in this order:

1. **User named them** → use those, but sanity-check each is a real alternative for the brand's buyer, not just a famous name in the space.
2. **competitors.md exists** → confirm the roster in one question ("Re-tear these five, or change the list?"). This is the only question the mode asks.
3. **Neither** → for a local service business, switch to **LOCAL** mode (review sites
   and "alternatives" searches don't list plumbers; the map does). Otherwise discover from the `Category:` line in `positioning#market-assessment`: search "best `<category>` tools", "`<category>` alternatives", and the G2/Capterra category page. Pick by ICP overlap, not size.

We use Exa for the discovery searches: it finds the pages a keyword search misses, such as a smaller peer or an up-and-comer (free tier, then pay as you go). Without it, the same searches in WebSearch work.

Roster judgment: one aspirational leader (sets the category's vocabulary), two or three true peers (fight for the same buyer this quarter), one up-and-comer (shows where the category is moving). A roster of five peers tells you nothing about trajectory; a roster of five giants tells you nothing actionable. More than six competitors dilutes the synthesis. Depth beats coverage.

### Phase 2: Parallel evidence collection

**Check the web first.** Phase 1's discovery search counts; otherwise run one WebSearch yourself before dispatching. If it is denied or errors, the subagents will be blocked too: don't dispatch. Write `competitors.md` from model knowledge instead (roster and known positioning, every price and count `UNVERIFIED`), labeled `Data: MODEL KNOWLEDGE (not checked live)` in the file, and say in one line in chat that allowing WebSearch and WebFetch (`/permissions`) and re-running makes it live.

Dispatch **one subagent per competitor, all in parallel** (Task tool, `general-purpose`). Budget per subagent: ≤ 40 fetches, ≤ 8 minutes, no sub-agents. Six surfaces is ~6-12 fetches, not a crawl. Each subagent gets the brief below plus the competitor's name and domain, and returns the evidence pack: facts, verbatim quotes, URLs. **No analysis in the packs**; synthesis happens centrally so claims can be compared across competitors. The packs are working data: save them to `./campaigns/competitive-intel/<date>-evidence.md` and never paste them into chat.

- We use Firecrawl for the page reads (`firecrawl_scrape`, `firecrawl_search`): full-page reads, including the JavaScript-rendered pricing pages that a plain fetch returns as a shell (free tier of 1,000 credits a month, no card). Without it, use WebFetch + WebSearch, and if a fetch returns a shell, pull the page from a search cache and say so.
- Enhanced (`SCRAPECREATORS_API_KEY` set): for creator, social, and ad-library recon,
  use only endpoints that ScrapeCreators documents at docs.scrapecreators.com;
  baseline: use WebFetch/WebSearch on public pages and report any gaps. Or treg, one token
  for many data APIs (pay per call), if you'd rather not open a separate account for social
  and ad data.
- Quotes are **verbatim**: exact headline text, exact price strings ("$49/mo billed annually"), exact CTA labels. Paraphrase destroys the synthesis (you can't cluster claims you've already rewritten).

# Content Atomizer

Turn one finished piece into the few platform-native assets it actually deserves, and nothing else. The judgment this skill carries: platform selection and native depth are the work; volume is the failure mode. Rephrased-spray content is a strategy for being ignored at scale; platform-specific evidence lives in `references/platform-facts.md`. This skill is a floor, not a ceiling. If the content in front of you deserves a better path than the one below, take it and say why in one line.

## Context

Only if `./brand/`, `./brands/` or `MARKETING.md` exists (nothing to load otherwise), run:
`python3 ${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/../start-here/scripts/brand_context.py --for content-atomizer`
(If the script or python3 is unavailable, read the files named in `reads:` directly, section-anchored where specified. If none exist, proceed standalone and ask only for what the task strictly requires.)

What each input does here:
- **voice-profile#platform-adaptations**: the per-platform voice table. It is the ONLY source of voice adjustment in this skill; never invent a parallel adaptation table. No profile means ask one question ("how formal, and any words you'd never use?") and write in a clean neutral register.
- **learnings**: platform performance priors. Apply them. Mention one only when it changed the work, as a single line in the note ("Your carousels outperformed text posts 3/3 in May, so LinkedIn gets one").
- **algo-cache**: per-brand dated platform facts, if /performance-review or a prior refresh has written any. Where it conflicts with this skill's reference file, the fresher `last-verified` wins.

**Freshness gate (run before generating):** load `references/platform-facts.md`. If today is past `last-verified + ttl-days`, refresh per the instruction in its header, update the file, and say so in one line in the note. Never generate against stale algorithm facts silently.

## Modes

| Mode | Trigger | Output |
|---|---|---|
| **Atomize** (default) | Source content + "repurpose / atomize / post from this" | 3-6 native pieces across 2-3 platforms |
| **Engagement replies** | "draft replies," pasted comments, a post URL + "respond" | Ranked reply drafts + relationship flags |
| **Calendar** | "content calendar," "week of posts from this" | Atomize output + dated `schedule.md` |
| **Full fan-out** | Explicit only: "all platforms," "everything," "max distribution" | Wide coverage, after a one-line warning |

Quick Mode applies: "give me an X post from this" means one X post, fast. Skip platform selection, skip the brief, deliver and lint it.

---

## Phase 1: Platform judgment (this is the skill)

Before writing anything, decide where this content should go and how deep. Two questions, in order.

### 1a. Which platforms does this brand operate?

Evidence, in priority order: filled rows in the voice-profile platform-adaptations table (an empty or templated row means they don't really post there), platform entries in learnings, platforms named in the request. If still unclear, ask ONE question: "Which 2-3 platforms do you actually post on?" Do not default to all eight. A platform the user doesn't operate gets nothing, because orphan posts on a dead account are worse than absence.

### 1b. What does THIS content deserve on each operated platform?

Per platform, assign one of four treatments:

- **Native deep**: the content's strongest material, rebuilt in the platform's native format from scratch. The piece should read like it was conceived for the platform.
- **Native light**: one standalone post carrying a single extractable insight.
- **Link-in-reply**: a self-contained post that delivers the core value, with the source link in the first reply (on X, links in the post body cost 30-50% of reach; see platform-facts). The post must work for someone who never clicks.
- **Skip**, and say why. "This has nothing for TikTok" is a correct, complete answer. Skipping is not under-delivery; spraying is.

Fit judgment by content shape:

| Source material | Strong fit | Weak fit |
|---|---|---|
| Framework / numbered process | LinkedIn carousel or document, X thread | Short video (compresses badly) |
| First-person story with a turn | X long-form post, LinkedIn text, TikTok/Reel script | Carousel (kills the pacing) |
| Original data / research | X post + chart, LinkedIn text, Reddit deep post | Instagram (unless /creative builds the visual) |
| Contrarian argument | X standalone post, Threads | LinkedIn (argue with evidence there, not edge) |
| Tutorial / how-to | TikTok/Shorts script, carousel | Threads, Bluesky |
| Opinion / commentary | Threads, X, Bluesky | YouTube |

**Default budget: 2-3 platforms, 1-2 pieces each (3-6 total).** Depth beats coverage. Every piece justifies itself by treatment, not quota; exceed the budget when the source and the brand's footprint genuinely earn it, stating why. Full fan-out only on explicit request, prefaced once with: "Heads up: broad fan-out of one source underperforms native depth on the platforms you actually run, and current rankers demote rephrased cross-posts. Doing it as asked."

State the plan in 3-5 lines (platform, treatment, why, plus skips with reasons) before generating. If the user redirects, that's the cheapest possible edit.

**Worked example** (illustrative; source: Hartline Plumbing's 2,400-word guide to water heater replacement costs in Dallas, a sample business; the brand operates LinkedIn + X and has a dormant Instagram):

```
Plan: "What a water heater swap actually cost our Dallas customers in 2026"
  LinkedIn   native deep   the cost-by-tank-size breakdown is carousel-shaped; your
                           carousels beat text 3/3 in May
  X          native light + link-in-reply   the headline number stands alone; the
                           job-by-job detail stays in the guide, linked in reply 1
  Instagram  skip          account dormant since March; cost charts need /creative
                           visuals to be worth posting there at all
3 pieces total. Say the word if you want wider coverage.
```

## Phase 2: Extract

Mine the source once, before writing anything. Pull only elements that survive standalone. If a point needs the surrounding article to make sense, it isn't an atom, it's a fragment.

- **Core insight**: the one sentence someone should repeat to a colleague
- **Supporting points**: 3-7, each carrying its own evidence
- **Stories**: concrete scenes with a turn, not "we learned a lot"
- **Data points**: specific numbers with their context attached
- **Contrarian takes**: positions a smart peer could actually dispute
- **Quotable lines**: sentences that earn a screenshot

If the source is a URL, fetch it (Firecrawl if `FIRECRAWL_API_KEY` is set, else WebFetch). For audio/video, work from the transcript and note timestamps next to extracted moments, because they become clip references.

# Creative Engine

One engine for every visual asset a brand ships. The judgment: match motion and style
to positioning, spend pennies finding direction before spending dollars on finals, and
never present an asset you haven't looked at yourself. Done = downloaded files,
QA-checked, brand-consistent, named so downstream skills can find them. This is the
floor, not the ceiling. When the situation argues for a better path, take it and say why.

## What we use

None of this is required. With no key, prompt-only mode writes the exact prompt, model
and settings for any tool you already have. When you want the files made for you, this is
the stack we run, one pick per job. Keys are listed in TOOLS.md; payloads and per-model
prices live only in `references/MODEL_REGISTRY.md`.

- **Images.** We use GPT Image 2.6 (OpenAI): Flare for fast drafts, Sunburst for finals and
  for keeping a product consistent across edits. It holds the `image-complex-prompt` and
  `image-instruct-edit` roles (exact layout, edits to a real photo, native-looking phone
  photos, animated GIFs). It is pay per image, through the OpenAI API (`OPENAI_API_KEY`) or
  Replicate. Everyday stills stay on `image-default`. Ad text is set in HTML over the image,
  not generated inside it. Without a key, the prompt-only deliverable works in any image tool.
- **Video.** We use Seedance 2.5 (ByteDance) through Higgsfield or Replicate, pay per

# Direct Response Copy

Copy that converts sounds like a smart friend explaining something they figured out,
while it quietly answers every doubt the reader has. This skill writes that copy in the
customer's own words, matches it to whatever sent the reader, keeps every claim to what
the business can back, and scores it privately before it ships. It's a floor, not a
ceiling. When the situation argues for a better path, take it and say why.

Frameworks (awareness levels, Schwartz, Caples, the seven scoring dimensions) are for
thinking. The copy, the notes and the chat summary say things in plain words, and scores
never appear in the deliverable unless the user asked for a score.

## Context

Only if `./brand/`, `./brands/` or `MARKETING.md` exists (nothing to load otherwise), run:
`python3 ${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/../start-here/scripts/brand_context.py --for direct-response-copy`
(`${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}` is this skill's folder; outside Claude Code use the folder this
file was read from, e.g. `.agents/skills/direct-response-copy`. If the script or python3 is
unavailable, read the brand folder directly: `./brands/<slug>/` when `./brands/active`
names one, else `./brand/`; then `MARKETING.md`, `preferences.md` and the files in
`reads:`. If none exist, proceed standalone and ask only for the offer, who it's for, and what proof exists.)

If `learnings.md` holds relevant priors (headline patterns, offers, past test results),
apply them and say which: "Applied: price-led headlines beat speed-led on your March
service pages."

## Entry points

| Request | Path |
|---|---|
| New copy (default) | Phases 0 to 5; for pages, then offer the /landing-page handoff |
| "Score this" or "why isn't this converting" | Load the copy and `references/calibration-anchors.md`, score, give the scorecard and the top fixes. Rewrite only if asked. A live URL goes to /landing-page TEARDOWN; a local business's phone-first check goes to /first-screen-check |
| Single quick asset (5 subject lines, one ad, a headline and first screen) | Quick Mode: skip the Phase 0 fan-out, brief.md and `./brand/assets.md`; generate, run the gate once, save the copy file, deliver |
| "Build the page" (copy approved) | Route to /landing-page BUILD FROM COPY |

**Iteration:** if `./campaigns/{name}/` already holds copy, read it first and ask: revise,
add a piece, or start fresh. When revising, score the existing copy first so the rewrite
targets real weaknesses.

## Phase 0. Find the words before writing any

Robert Collier's rule: enter the conversation already going on in the reader's mind. The
best headlines are usually found, often verbatim, in customer language.

1. **Read `./brand/voc.md` and `positioning#chosen-angle` if they exist.** Pull verbatim
   pains, desires and objections. "I'm doing my books at midnight on the 30th" is a
   headline; "users struggle with bookkeeping" is not.
2. **If voc.md is absent and a product URL exists**, run a quick parallel pass, 2-3
   subagents at once: the product or service page (claims, pricing, mechanism, who it's
   for); 1-2 competitor pages (the saturated promises your copy must not sound like); one
   review source that fits (G2, an app store, Amazon or a Reddit thread for products;
   Yelp, BBB or review snippets for a local business). Each returns verbatim quotes with
   URLs, not prose. WebFetch and WebSearch do this for free. We use Firecrawl to read the
   pages in full (free tier of 1,000 credits a month, no card) and Exa to find the
   competitor and review pages a keyword search misses (free tier, then pay as you go).
   Without them the free tools read what they can reach. Park findings in `./campaigns/{name}/brief.md` (full runs only).
3. **If neither exists**, write from the user's input, label the deliverable
   `Data: MODEL KNOWLEDGE (verify claims before spending)`, and suggest /audience-research
   to build voc.md. Point at `preferences.md` or `MARKETING.md` for banned words by name;
   never restate a banned phrase.

Label mined deliverables `Data: LIVE (n sources)`.

## Phase 1. Frame the job

First time? `references/worked-example.md` shows three before-and-afters (a local
service, a SaaS, a coach) so you can see the bar. Establish five things. Ask only for
what's missing.

**Format.** Landing page (one offer, one primary CTA, scannable), sales page (long-form,
story-driven, full objection handling), email (one idea, one CTA, the subject line is the
headline), ad, social post, text message, or other. For ads and social, don't trust
remembered character limits: pull current limits from `voice-profile#platform-adaptations`
or `./brand/algo-cache.md`, and refresh per its TTL if stale.

**Where the reader came from, and what they were promised.** A reader arrives carrying a
promise from the ad, email, post or search that sent them. The first screen has to repeat
that promise in the same words, or they leave. Get the ad text, keyword, subject line or
post, and write the headline to match it. Local businesses miss this constantly.
In a check of local sites on a phone (Nov 2026), most businesses running ads that promise 24/7 or same-day service didn't say it on the first screen of the page the ad opens.

**Awareness level (Schwartz).** This decides the lead:

| Level | They know | Lead with |
|---|---|---|
| 1 Unaware | nothing | identity, emotion, story |
| 2 Problem-aware | the pain | the problem named vividly, then that a fix exists |
| 3 Solution-aware | fixes exist | your unique mechanism |
| 4 Product-aware | your product | differentiation, proof, objections handled |
| 5 Most-aware | they want it | the offer itself |

Less aware means longer copy. Most-aware means get out of the way.

**The so-what chain.** Ask "so what?" of every feature until you reach time, money or
worry, usually three levels down: "automatic reminders" so "invoices get paid without you
asking" so "you stop sending awkward emails to clients you like". Write from the bottom.

**Fact sheet and proof inventory.** List every fact the copy may use, each with its
source: the brief or the user's messages, the business's site, its reviews, or research
you verified. Then what proof exists: testimonials, data, case studies, review counts,
photos, credentials. Never write a claim bigger than its proof. If the proof is thin, the
copy gets quieter, not louder. Pull the angle from `positioning#chosen-angle`; if none
exists and the market is saturated, suggest /positioning-angles first.

lost. This skill designs the sequence that bridges it, sized and paced to the offer,
written in the brand's voice with the customer's words, and checks the real sending

# Find Local Clients

This skill takes one trade in one town and ranks every business in it by how many customers it is losing, with a can-pay tier and the one problem worth pitching. Done means a list an agency could start emailing tomorrow, where every row names its biggest problem in the owner's words and carries evidence someone else can re-check in two minutes.

The best prospect is not the worst business. It is an established business that already gets demand (reviews, ads, a crew to feed) and leaks it at a step you can fix and prove. A 3.4-star shop has a problem with the work, not the marketing. A business with no reviews and no site can't pay. The sweet spot is a busy business that already pays for marketing and loses customers close to the phone. This is a floor, not a ceiling. When the town in front of you argues for a better path, take it and say why in one line.

## Context

If none exist, proceed standalone and ask only for the trade, the town, and, if they want, what they sell.)

The brand files here are the agency's own. `positioning#chosen-angle` says what the agency sells, so problems it can fix rank above problems it can't. If `learnings.md` has `[find-local-clients]` or `[pitch-the-fix]` entries (which problems got replies), apply them. One line in the note, and only if one changed a ranking or a pick.

Prospect facts go in the campaign folder only. Never save a business, an owner or a score to the assistant's own memory or notes (prospect data stays in the workspace). Before any fan-out, run one WebSearch in the main thread. If it is denied, work only from a list the user provides and say so in the note. Never build a business list from model knowledge; a list from memory is an invented list.

## Phase 1: Pick the cell

A cell is one trade in one town. Default size: 40 to 120 businesses. Smaller and the ranking means little; bigger and the hand checks in Phase 4 take all week. A big metro needs narrowing to a county, a suburb cluster or one side of town.

If the user hasn't picked a trade, apply three checks and recommend one:

1. **Ticket size.** A job worth $500 or more, or work that recurs (maintenance plans, cleanings). One extra job a month has to pay your fee in the owner's head.
2. **Urgency.** Emergencies and seasons force a fast call, so a leak at the phone costs real money. Plumbing, HVAC, roofing after storms, garage doors, restoration, towing, locksmiths.
3. **Owner-run.** Crews of about 3 to 30 with one decision maker. Franchise locations often can't touch their own site or ads; list them, but mark them `franchise` and keep them out of the top ten unless the user sells to franchisees.

Write the cell to `./campaigns/prospects-{trade}-{town}/cell.md`: trade, town and its edges, the search phrases you'll use, and today's date. That file is also the working log: the searches run, sources skipped, and which fields were checked by hand for which businesses. It is saved, not pasted.

## Phase 2: Gather the businesses

Free sources, in the order that gives the cleanest list. Load `references/free-sources-facts.md` for the details and the dated facts behind each one.

1. **The state license list**, where the trade is licensed. It is the most complete list there is and it names the license holder, who is often the owner. Some boards publish the whole list as a free download; Texas plumbing is one.
2. **Search results.** WebSearch 4 to 6 phrasings a customer would type: "[trade] [town]", "emergency [trade] [town]", "[trade] near [neighborhood]", "best [trade] in [town]", plus the money service ("water heater replacement [town]"). Record names, sites and phones.
3. **Directories.** BBB (years in business, management names, complaint count), the trade association's member directory, the Chamber of Commerce, Angi and Nextdoor where they load. Yelp often blocks fetches; skip it when it does and say so.
4. **Optional: the Google Places API** with the user's own key. It is the terms-friendly way to pull rating, review count, website, phone and open-or-closed for the whole cell in one run: `python3 ${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/places_search.py "plumber in Dallas, TX" "emergency plumber Dallas, TX" > places.csv`. **Hard rule:** no Google Maps scrapers (Apify, Outscraper, home-made bots), no logged-in tricks, no bulk automated browsing of Maps. Google's terms forbid scraping Maps content. # First Screen Check

Most local customers meet a business on a phone, from a Google search, a map listing or
an ad, and decide in the first screen whether to call, go back, or call the next
result. This skill looks at that screen the way they do and reports what's missing,
ranked by how many calls it costs, with one fix to make first. Done means a short list
an owner can act on today, each item backed by what the page actually shows. The checks
are a floor. When the business in front of you argues for a different order, change it
and say why.

## Context

Only if `./brand/`, `./brands/` or `MARKETING.md` exists (nothing to load otherwise), run:
`python3 ${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/../start-here/scripts/brand_context.py --for first-screen-check`
(`${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}` is this skill's folder; outside Claude Code use the folder this
file was read from, e.g. `.agents/skills/first-screen-check`. If the script or python3 is
unavailable, read the brand folder directly: `./brands/<slug>/` when `./brands/active`
names one, else `./brand/`; then `MARKETING.md`, `preferences.md` and the files in
`reads:`. If none exist, proceed standalone. Ask only for the URL, and for the
ad's text if the page is an ad's landing page.)

Checking a prospect's site rather than the user's own? Don't load or write brand files
for it. The report lands in `./campaigns/` and nothing else changes.

No URL given, or only a placeholder (example.com, yourdomain.com)? Ask for the URL in one
line. Never run the checks or the redirect and structured-data commands against a
placeholder.

## What the data says

From hundreds of local business sites checked on a phone in November 2026.
The sample is self-selected (businesses that people chose to look up, mostly US home
services), so read the shares as "common", not as a census.

- Very few passed every check. Most had 3 or more gaps.
- Most businesses running ads that promise 24/7 or same-day service don't say it on the first screen of the page the ad opens, and many never say it anywhere on that page.
- Most have 4.5 stars or better and 100 or more reviews, and most of those don't show the rating on the first screen.

The common failures aren't about design taste. They are things the business already has (a promise it pays to advertise, a rating it earned) that never
reach the screen where the customer decides. Look for those first.

## Phase 1: Pick the page and the promise

**The page.** Check the page customers actually land on, not the one the owner thinks
of as "the site". In order of how much traffic it usually carries:

1. The page each ad opens (its final URL). Paid clicks are the most expensive visitors.
2. The page the Google Business Profile's website button opens (often the homepage,
   sometimes a location page).
3. The page that ranks for "<main service> <city>".

If several differ, check the ad page and the profile page. Two good checks beat five
thin ones.

**The promise.** Write down, word for word, what the customer was promised before
they tapped: the ad's headline and description, the profile's hours ("Open 24 hours"),
and any offer ("$49 drain cleaning", "free estimates"). Free ways to get the ad text:

- The user pastes it, or a screenshot from their ad account.
- Google's Ads Transparency Center (adstransparency.google.com): search the business
  name or domain, set the region, and read the text ads. It searches by advertiser, not
  by keyword.
- A search for "<service> <city>" on a phone in the service area. Ads change by location
  and hour, so say when and where you looked.

No ad running? The promise is whatever the profile and the search snippet said:
the hours, the services, the rating shown beside the listing.

## Phase 2: See the first screen on a phone

Take the best path the agent has. The report says only whether it rests on a phone
screenshot or on the page HTML.

**A. A browser on the machine (best).** Playwright takes a phone-size screenshot from
the command line. The first time on a machine, download its browser with
`npx playwright install chromium`; without it the screenshot command fails with
"Executable doesn't exist".

```bash
npx playwright install chromium   # once per machine
npx playwright screenshot --viewport-size "390,664" --wait-for-timeout 3000 --timeout 45000 <url> first-screen.png
npx playwright screenshot --viewport-size "390,664" --full-page --timeout 45000 <url> full-page.png
```

390 by 664 is what an iPhone 13 shows inside the browser bars. The 3-second wait lets
late popups, chat bubbles and cookie banners load, because the customer sees those too.
(`--device "iPhone 13"` also works but runs WebKit, which needs
`npx playwright install webkit` first.) Read both images. Count how many phone screens
tall the full page is and where the number, the promise and the rating first appear.

A browser extension or MCP browser works the same way: set the window to 390 wide,
load, wait, capture.

**B. No browser, Firecrawl keyed.** We use Firecrawl for this: its scrape returns a
phone-size screenshot and the rendered HTML with no browser installed, and it reads pages
that build themselves with JavaScript (free tier of 1,000 credits a month, no card). Ask for
the mobile screenshot and the rendered HTML. Same reading as A. Without it, path A or C
does the same check.

**C. Neither (fallback).** Read the HTML in order. If python3 is available, run:

```bash
python3 ${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/page_facts.py <url> --promise "24/7" --promise "same-day"
```

word and "reviews" first appear (as a word position), forms and their fields, the
structured data, the weight of the first images, and widgets that tend to cover the
screen. Without python3, WebFetch the page and read the same things by hand.

**Estimating the first screen from HTML.** It usually holds the header, the headline and
somewhere between 20 and 70 words of copy, fewer when a big photo, video or offer banner

first screen. In Sources and assumptions, say once in plain words that the first screen is

# Google Ads Tracking

Google Ads can only bid toward what it can see. In most local service accounts it sees
calls tapped inside the ad, a stray offline upload and Google's own Business Profile
actions, and nothing from the person who clicked the ad, read the page and called.
This skill finds what is counted, decides what should bid, fixes the tag, and proves the
fix with a recorded conversion. Done means every lead path is counted once, the actions
that bid are real leads that fire often enough to learn from, and the budget call rests on
impression share, not a hunch. The method is a floor: when the account in front of you
argues for a better path, take it and say why in one line.

Two hard rules:

1. **Nothing changes in the account without a yes for that exact change.** Show the object,
   the field, before and after. Never press "Apply all" on Recommendations.
2. **A fix is proven by data, not by a saved setting.** The repair is done when the new
   action records a real conversion from ad traffic, usually within 7 days. A green tag
   check proves the tag loads. It does not prove Google counts the lead.

## Context

Only if `./brand/`, `./brands/` or `MARKETING.md` exists (nothing to load otherwise), run:
`python3 ${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/../start-here/scripts/brand_context.py --for google-ads-tracking`
(`${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}` is this skill's folder; outside Claude Code use the folder this
file was read from, e.g. `.agents/skills/google-ads-tracking`. If the script or python3 is
unavailable, read the brand folder directly: `./brands/<slug>/` when `./brands/active`
names one, else `./brand/`; then `MARKETING.md`, `preferences.md` and the files in
`reads:`. If none exist, proceed standalone and ask only for: the site URL, how leads arrive (calls,
forms, booking), whether the phone number on the site is the real number or a tracking
number, and view access to Google Ads.)

**Load `references/google-ads-facts.md` first** and check its header. UI labels, call
tracking options and API enums drift. If today is past last-verified plus ttl-days,
refresh it per its instruction; if that isn't possible, the Sources and assumptions note
says the UI labels are as of last-verified.

Sample used below: **Hartline Plumbing, Dallas TX (hartlineplumbing.com), a sample
business.** About 40 leads a month, most by phone, a quote form few people use.

## Modes

| Say | What runs |
|---|---|
| Nothing | All five phases in order. Every account change waits for a yes (hard rule 1). |
| `audit` | Phases 1 to 3 plus the read half of Phase 5 (bid strategy, impression share). Read only: nothing in the account changes. |
| `fix` | Phase 4, using the plan from an earlier audit. With no audit on file it runs Phases 1 to 3 first. Ends when the 7-day proof is in. |
| `budget` | Phase 5, for an account whose tracking is already proven. If Phase 4 isn't proven yet, it says so and starts there. |

## Phase 1: Map the lead paths (10 minutes)

List every way a customer becomes a lead after seeing an ad, and what in Google Ads
should count it. Fill this in for the business before opening the account:

| Path | What the customer does | Counted by |
|---|---|---|
| Call from the ad | Taps the call button on the ad or the location asset | "Calls from ads" |
| Click, then tap the number | Clicks the ad, lands on the site, taps the phone number on a phone | A website call action set to "Someone makes a call by clicking a number on my website" |
| Click, then dial | Reads the number on a desktop or copies it, dials later | A forwarding-number action ("Someone calls a number shown on my website") or a call tracking tool's number, sent to Google Ads |
| Click, then form | Submits the quote form | A website action that fires on confirmed success |
| Click, then book | Books in an online scheduler | A website action on the scheduler's booking-confirmed event |
| Saw the ad, called from the Business Profile | Finds the profile later and calls | "Calls from ads" when the profile is linked and call history is on, plus local actions ("Clicks to call", "Get directions") when location assets run |
| Became a paid job | Booked and paid | An offline upload from the job or invoicing system, days later |

Then ask the owner one number: **how many calls and form leads did the business get last
month, from the phone system and the inbox, not from Google?** That is the yardstick for
Phase 2. Without it, a Google conversion count can't be judged as too low or too high.

## Phase 2: Read what Google sees (free, Google Ads UI)

1. **Goals > Conversions > Summary.** For every conversion action record, in
   `./campaigns/<business-slug>/notes.md` (working data, not pasted): name,
   source (website, calls from ads, Google hosted, import), category, Primary or
   Secondary, the Tracking status column, conversions and all conversions for the last 30
   and 90 days, count setting, click-through window.
2. **Which goals bid.** Note which goals are account-default, then open each campaign's
   settings and check whether it uses account-default goals or its own.
3. **Campaigns table.** Add the columns Bid strategy type, Conversions, All conv., Search
   impr. share, Search lost IS (rank), Search lost IS (budget).
4. **Compare** the primary conversion count with the owner's lead count from Phase 1.
